samāpatti
(‘attaining identity [with the object of concentration]’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras (1.41). Literally, it means attaining identity (āpatti) totally (sam) with the object of concentration. It refers to the state that the मिन्द् attains.
When the चित्त or the मिन्द् loses its vṛttis or modifications raised by तमस् and रजस् through yogic disciplines, and becomes absolutely pure like a colourless crystal, becomes one with the object of concentration, it is said to have attained समापत्ति. This is like the pure crystal totally reflecting a red hibiscus flower kept near it, as if losing its own identity in the process.
This is practically the same as समाधि.

Samayācāryas
(‘teachers of [Śiva] tradition’)
------------------------------------------
Śaivism is a very ancient religion (or sect) of India. The sixty-three Nāyanmārs (‘servants of God’) of Tamil Nadu as also the Śivaśaraṇas of Karnataka are its prominent teachers.
The four most important ācāryas or teachers of Tamil शैविस्म् are generally known as समयाचार्यस् (‘teachers who knew the samaya or tradition, best’). They are: अप्पर्, ज्ञानसम्बन्धर्, Sundara-mūrti and माणिक्कवाचगर्.
(See under each name for details.)

samāhartṛ
(‘one who brings revenue’)
------------------------------------------
Kauṭilya (300 B. C.) in his monumental work, the Arthaśāstra, has described in detail, an ideal system of administration of a State.
One of the important officers of the State is the समाहर्तृ (the Collector-General). He divides the kingdom into four districts, arranges the villages into three grades and supervises over the collection of various taxes and revenues from forts, rural areas, mines, embankments, forests, herds of cattle and roads for traffic (vide 2.6 and 2.35).
See also ARTHAŚĀSTRA.

śamitṛ
(‘one who silences [the animal victim]’)
------------------------------------------
In the Somayāgas of the पशुबन्ध type where an animal is sacrificed, the person who kills the animal by suffocating or strangulating it is called a शमितृ. He may be a trained butcher or even the अध्वर्यु priest himself.
In the place—a previously arranged spot—where the severed limbs of the victim are to be roasted, a new fire is to be lighted. It is called śāmitra. This fire may be produced newly by attrition or by drawing it from the आहवनीय fire itself.

sāman
------------------------------------------
The word सामन् refers to the Sāmaveda as also its mantras. (See SĀMAVEDA for details.)
Sāman is also one of the four upāyas or means available to the kings while dealing with others. In general, it means to cement the bonds of friendship with the person who should not be alienated.
This can be done in five ways: by recounting the good turns done by each to the other; by praising the qualities and actions of the other person who is to be won over; declaring the relationship of each other; representing the good that will result in future; declaring ‘I am yours and I am at your service.’ (Kāmandakīya-nītisāra 17.4 and 5).

samādhāna
(‘keeping [the मिन्द्] well-established [in the आत्मन् or God]’)
------------------------------------------
Advaita Vedānta describes a four-fold sādhana (spiritual discipline) generally called साधनचतुष्टय. The third step, the शमादिषट्क (the group of six steps), includes समाधान as the last item. It is concentration of मिन्द् on the object of contemplation.
(See SĀDHANACATUṢṬAYA.)
This word is also used to indicate a suitable or satisfactory reply given to a doubt or a query or an objection raised in philosophical disputations.
In a more general sense, it means pacification of an aggrieved party.

Sāmbapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
This is an upapurāṇa (minor or secondary purāṇa) belonging to the Saura group (devoted to Sun-worship). It might have been composed during the period A.

-800.
Sāmba was the son of कृष्ण from his wife Jāmbavatī. He is said to have established a temple for सूर्य or Sun-god at the city Sāmbapura built by him. He brought eighteen families of Magi priests from Śākadvīpa and handed over the regular worship of सूर्य to them.
This work contains many interesting stories. Other details dealt with are: च्रेअतिओन्; the solar system; eclipses; geography of the earth; description of the deity सूर्य and his attendants; on images of these deities; some details about योग; on mantras and their use; customs and manners; certain rites and rituals; results of actions.

Samayācāra Tantra
------------------------------------------
The Samayācāra Tantra is considered as an important work among the 64 तन्त्रस्. Spread over 281 verses in the anuṣṭubh metre it deals with all aspects of tantra literature, though briefly.
Practices of वामाचार (See under TANTRAS.) find a prominent place.
The word ‘samayācāra’ refers to the system of worship and allied details, as applied to a specified deity.
It also means the देवी or the Divine मोथेर्.
Some of the topics dealt with in this work may now be described briefly: materials to be used in worship as also those which can be consumed after offering; various times of the day suitable for different rites with specific results like śāntikarmas (rites for peace) or vaśya-कर्म (getting others under one’s control) and so on; the various āsanas or postures to be adopted according to the results desired, like पद्मासन in peace-rites; certain aspects of the theory involving the books and deities of this school; certain types of mālās (rosaries) and the results of using them; various types of āsanas or seats and the results of their use as for instance the tiger-skin being used if one wants मोक्ष (liberation); descriptions of places suitable for the performance of जप (repetition of मन्त्र); classification of mantras as puṁ (male), स्त्री (female) and napuṁsaka (neuter); two types of practices, वामाचार and dakṣiṇācara (the left-hand and the right-hand paths); qualities of a गुरु or teacher and the शिष्य or disciple; various articles needed for पूजा especially the ones known as पञ्चमकारस् (See TANTRAS.); description of pīṭhas or seats suitable for the performance of जप, they being the शक्ति-pīṭhas, places hallowed by the body-parts of Satī—Dākṣāyaṇī (See TANTRAS); giving of balis (ceremonial offerings) to various deities; certain mantras concerning the various aspects of शिव like अघोर; and methods of purifying mantras known as मन्त्रसṁस्कार (See MANTRASAṀSKĀRA for details).
Though a small work, it contains a lot of information about the practical aspects of तन्त्रस्, more attention being given to the वामाचार practices.

Samantapañcaka
(‘the place surrounded by five [lakes]’)
------------------------------------------
See KURUKṢETRA.

Sampāti
------------------------------------------
Sampāti and जटायु, the two great eagles mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa, were brothers and were the sons of अरुण, the charioteer of सूर्य (the Sun-god).
Once both of them started flying towards the sun. As they flew nearer the sun, the heat became so intense that it became unbearable. सम्पाति, to protect his younger brother जटायु, spread his wings over him thereby getting them burnt.
When the sage चन्द्र heard his story, he told him that he would get back his wings when, in future, he would reveal the place where सीता was kept, to the monkey army of राम. This he did and got back his wings.
See also JAṬĀYU.

samādhi
(‘state of perfect concentration’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) deals with the techniques of controlling and concentrating the मिन्द्. The work gives eight steps—generally known as aṣṭāṅgas (hence the name Aṣṭāṅgayoga for पतञ्जलि’s system)—out of which the last three are धारणा, ध्यान and समाधि.
Dhāraṇā is the fixing of attention on a definite locus, such as the lotus of the heart, the light in the brain, the tip of the nose or the tongue, or on an external object like the मोओन् or the image of gods and so on.
When धारणा ripens so that the flow of the thought-current becomes unbroken, it becomes ध्यान. Here the मिन्द् hovers round the object of meditation. There is still the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the trio—the ego-sense, the object of meditation and the process of meditation.
When again ध्यान becomes perfect and the मिन्द् is so deeply absorbed in the object that it loses itself and has no awareness of itself, the state attained is called समाधि. In this state, only the object of meditation will be shining in the मिन्द् and the योगि is not even aware of the thought process involved in it. Even the ego-sense is completely subjugated.
In the state of समाधि, which is an intuitive and superconscious experience, the object of meditation will reveal all its secrets to the योगि. If the योगि can make his own self or ईश्वर the object of meditation after learning about them from the Sāṅkhya (an allied philosophical system declaring the knowledge of the Self as the means of लिबेरतिओन्), he will get कैवल्य (liberation). पतञ्जलि calls these two samādhis respectively as सम्प्रज्ञात and असम्प्रज्ञात. In the former, the object of meditation is known in its entirety. In the latter nothing outside the Self is known (samprajñāta = well-known, असम्प्रज्ञात = not known).
See also NIRVIKALPA.
Samādhi is the name of a वैश्य (merchant) who too received the esoteric teaching concerning the greatness of देवी, the Divine मोथेर्, along with the king सुरथ, from the sage सुमेधस्. He had been driven out of his home by his own greedy wife and children.
When he strayed into the hermitage of the sage, he met the king सुरथ. Both of them then approached the sage for consolation. By his teaching समाधि was guided towards मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्.
See DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA.

samudrayāna
(‘travel by sea’)
------------------------------------------
It is rather strange that some of the धर्मशास्त्रस् prohibited समुद्रयान (voyage by sea) for the dvijas in general and the ब्राह्मणस् in particular, by including it in the long list of what they call ‘kalivarjya’ (that which should be prohibited in the age of कलि, starting from 3100 B. C.) (Vide बौधायन धर्म-sūtras

; Manusmṛti 3.158 and 166, 167).
The fear of वर्णसङ्कर (mixing up of castes) was, perhaps, uppermost in their minds.
It is an undeniable fact that many sages and savants like अगस्त्य had travelled to foreign countries including the Middle East and the Far East. They went out, sans the Sword and sans the Book, to spread knowledge and the message of universal brotherhood.
Sea-voyage was quite flourishing even in the pre-Christian era. Trade and commerce contacts had been established with several countries both in the east and in the west.
The Vijayanagar empire itself boasted of 300 ports!

Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
This is one of the nine ब्राह्मणस् of the Sāmaveda available now.
It has three prapāṭhakas or prakaraṇas or chapters, known respectively as Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra and Kṛcchrātikṛcchra.
The first two have eight anuvākas (subsections) each and the last, nine.
Unlike the other works of Vedic literature, this ब्राह्मण does not deal with sacrifices at all. For the benefit of those who cannot perform वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् to get what they want, it prescribes several kṛcchras or rites of a magical nature, using the appropriate sāmans as the mantras. Hence it looks like a fore-runner of several topics dealt with in the later dharmaśāstra and tāntrik literature.
These topics may now be summarised briefly as follows:
Kṛcchra-prapāṭhaka
Anuvāka 1 : च्रेअतिओन् of the world from ब्रह्मा; in praise of sāmans that can grant whatever we want; a brief account of yajñas in general.
Anuvāka 2 : Description of the kṛcchras of various types along with the rules to be followed.
Anuvāka 3 : Rules guiding Vedic studies; results of some sacrifices like Pavamāneṣṭi.
Anuvāka 4 : Rite spread over seven nights (saptarātrika); the various sāmans to be used in getting the fruits of some sacrifices like अग्निष्टोम, अतिरात्र and Sattrayāgas; sāmans to be recited to please the deities like रुद्र, विष्णु, and विनायक as also for attaining मोक्ष.
Anuvāka 5 : Some prāyaścittas or expiations including the sāmans to be chanted.
Anuvākas 6, 7 and 8 : Some more expiations for sins like accepting prohi-bited gifts, killing a cow, selling things which should not be sold, evil द्रेअम्स् and so on.
Atikṛcchra Prapāṭhaka
Anuvāka 1 : Sāmans to be employed for attaining long life; purification of oneself; going to ब्रह्मलोक after death; gaining good health.
Anuvākas 2 to 8 : These prescribe the जप of various sāmans for the destruction of sins, for easy and safe delivery of babies, for getting a good son, for eliminating the evil effects brought about by malignant spirits, for removing the effects of poisons, for safe पिल्ग्रिमगे, for attaining fame or any other desire and so on.
Kṛcchrātikṛcchra Prapāṭhaka
All the nine anuvākas deal with similar topics such as: sāmans to be used for attaining wealth; how to perform vāstuhoma; how to discover hidden wealth; means of getting a vision of any deity; means of controlling the minds of others; and sādhana for obtaining मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
The work traces the paramparā (tradition) of teaching thus: ब्रह्मा to बृहस्पति; बृहस्पति to नारद; नारद to व्यास, and व्यास to जैमिनि.
It has two commentaries:
Vedārthaprakāśa by सायण (A.

-1387).
Padārthamātravivṛti by Bharatasvāmin (A.

sāmidhenī
(‘related to समिध् [or sacrificial fuel-stick]’)
------------------------------------------
When the दर्शपूर्णमास sacrifice is being performed, at a particular stage, eleven (or fifteen) mantras from the Ṛgveda are chanted to kindle the fire. These are known as the सामिधेनी verses.
They are: 3.27.1; 6.16.10-12; 3.27.13-15; 1.12.1; 3.27.4; 5.28.5-6.
Though these are eleven mantras, by repeating the first and the last verses twice each, the total becomes fifteen.
All of them are addressed to the deity अग्नि requesting him to burn more brilliantly and carry the offerings to the Vedic gods.
A समिध् (fuel-stick) is offered into the fire after each मन्त्र.

śama
(‘peace’)
------------------------------------------
Treatises on Vedānta deal with the sādhanas or means of attaining मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
In Advaita Vedānta the preliminary step is known as साधनचतुष्टय or four means. Out of these four, the third is शमादिषट्क or ṣaṭsampatti or the group of six disciplines beginning with शम. शम is defined as the internal peace or quietude got by preventing the मिन्द् from rushing towards the sense-objects that disturb it.
See SĀDHANACATUṢṬAYA.

sāmaga
(‘one who sings the sāma’)
------------------------------------------
A sāma (or सामन्) is any मन्त्र of the Ṛgveda set to tune as per the rules given in works like the Nāradīyaśikṣā. The Sāmaveda is full of such sāmas.
A सामग in general, is one who sings the sāma. All the four priests of the Sāmaveda, viz., the उद्गातृ, the प्रस्तोतृ, the pratihartṛ and the सुब्रह्मण्य, are sāmagas, though the उद्गातृ is the chief among them.
Chanting of a sāma needs specialised training.
A सामग should have a musical voice and a fine sense of śruti or tuning (of his voice to a basic note). He should chant in a medium tone—neither too loud not too low—uttering the words clearly and without tremour. He should know where the words have to be paused and must never make a mistake of the स्वर (intonation). Those who cannot chant in this way, should never attempt to learn it!
Sāmaga is also one of the names of विष्णु as given in the Viṣṇusaharanāma (number 575). Śrī कृष्ण declares that he is सामवेद among the Vedas (Bhagavad-gītā 10-22). Hence one who sings this Veda—the sāmaga—has practically identi-fied himself with the Lord in ecstasy.

śamādiṣaṭka
(‘the group of six [disciplines]’ starting with शम’)
------------------------------------------
This is the third of the four spiritual disciplines listed under साधनचतुष्टय. It consists of the following six steps: शम (tranquillity); दम (self-control); उपरति (cessation of external sense-organs from the pursuit of sense-objects); तितिक्षा (forbearance); श्रद्धा (faith) and samā-dhāna (concentration).

sampradāya
(‘that which is given or handed over [in succession]’)
------------------------------------------
Sampradāya or tradition, wherein a knowledge or a way of life is handed over from a गुरु (teacher) to a disciple or a group of disciples has a very important place in हिन्दुइस्म्.
Many a time, a गुरु does not impart all that he knows, to his disciples. From among those who live with him and serve him, he may choose one or two as the fittest to receive that knowledge he has kept back. It is this that often matters, more than the open teaching or the books. Because of this reason, सम्प्रदाय is all important.
A peculiar trait of हिन्दुइस्म् is that all sciences and arts are often traced to God Himself as the originator. Sometimes it may be a great ṛṣi or sage also.
‘Sampradāya’ may also mean the body of the founder-teachers and their immediate disciples.
There are different sampradāyas in each of the sciences or arts or fields of wisdom.
It is strongly believed that those mantras which are not handed down through a सम्प्रदाय, are useless and hence do not produce their results.
Some works like the Śaktisaṅgama-tantra (1.8) give long lists of sampradāyas such as Vaikhāna, Rādhāvallabhī, Pāñca-rātra, Vīravaiṣṇava, भागवत, निम्बार्क and Vṛndāvanī.

samidh
(‘that which burns brightly’)
------------------------------------------
Offering fuel-sticks, generally called समिध्, into a duly consecrated fire is a part and parcel of many a Hindu rite.
Some of the trees from which these sticks could be procured are: अश्वत्थ, (Ficus religiosa), बिल्व (Aegle marmelos), चन्दन (sandal-wood), devadāru (pine), khadira (Acacia catechu), nyagrodha (Indian fig-tree) and palāśa (Butea frondosa).
Fuel-sticks of certain trees like bibhī-taka (Terminalia bellerica), kapittha (wood-apple tree) and nimba (neem-tree) should not be used.
The sticks should not be thicker than the thumb, must have the bark on them and should not be worm-eaten. The size is prādeśa (one span). There should be no branches.

samabhaṅga
(‘symmetrical posture’)
------------------------------------------
See BHAṄGA.

Samayamata
------------------------------------------
This is another name for Samayācāra. See under TANTRAS.

Śampākagītā
(‘didactic poem of Śampāka’)
------------------------------------------
The celebrated Bhagavadgītā has inspired the composition of many more such gītās. They are found mostly in the Mahābhārata itself as also the Bhāgavata. A few have been discovered to be independent works.
The Śampākagītā, comprising just 22 verses, is a part of the Mahābhārata (Śāntiparva 176).
Yudhiṣṭhira poses a question to भीष्म as to the fate that overtakes a man, whether he is rich or poor. भीष्म recounts from his memory what he had heard once from Śampāka, a ब्राह्मण who was leading a life of त्याग or वैराग्य (renunciation).
None in this world is always happy or always suffering without experiencing the other state.
To get true happiness and peace, it is not enough to give up desires. One should strive for श्रेयस्, what is spiritually benefitting.
Duties and responsibilities of a king (or a ruler) weigh heavily on the मिन्द्. That naturally disturbs the मिन्द् and makes it go out of control.
Akiñcanatva, not possessing anything, is the best way to peace in life.
A man of total renunciation who does not keep any money or possessions, has nothing to fear. He is fully free, whereas a rich man lives in misery, being constantly overcome by anger, greed, delusion, pride and arrogance. These make him transgress all norms of धर्म and hence a victim of the ruler’s wrath.
Hence one should give up all kinds of worldly desires and find the true remedy to dispel sorrows and sufferings through spiritual wisdom.
It is त्याग (renunciation) and त्याग alone that gives us fearlessness and happiness, and takes to paramapada or the highest abode (liberation).

Sāmaveda
------------------------------------------
Introduction
The Sāmaveda or the Sāmaveda saṁhitā is the third in the traditional list of the four वेदस्. It comprises mostly the Ṛgvedic mantras (or ṛks)—1504 to be specific—set to the saptasvara system (the seven basic notes of Indian मुसिच्), to be sung at appropriate places in a sacrifice. It is the उद्गातृ (the third of the four major priests) along with his three assistants (prastotṛ, pratihartṛ and subrah-maṇya) that does this. The total number of ṛks in this Veda as per one calculation is 1875.
It should be noted that this Veda has been eulogised highly in the other वेदस् also (vide Ṛgveda 1.107.2; 2.43.2; 5.44.14. Atharvaveda 2.7.24; 7.54.1; 10.7.20). कृष्ण while describing his special aspects, says in the Bhagavadgītā (10.22) that he is Sāmaveda among the वेदस्.
Commentators of the Sāmaveda
The वेदस् are difficult to comprehend not only because of their archaic language but also because of their close association with the system of यज्ञ or sacrifice. Hence, the help of bhāṣyas or commentaries by those scholars, who also have an intimate knowledge of the Vedic tradi-tions, is invaluable.
The following are the commentators on the Sāmaveda whose works are available even now, though some of these are still in the form of manuscripts:
Mādhava Paṇḍita (A.

-1387)
Śobhākara Bhaṭṭa (circa A.

)
Sūryadaivajña (circa A.

)

Meaning of Sāma
The etymological meaning of the word sāma is ‘that which destroys sorrow by its sweetness; a song’.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad defines the sāma as a ṛk (Ṛgvedic मन्त्र) set to various tunes of मुसिच् (vide

).
Thus the sāmas are those mantras of the Ṛgveda which had been set to the tunes as prescribed by the special treatises like the Nāradīyaśīkṣā.
However, the same ṛk can be sung in different tunes thus producing different sāmas. The number of such sāmas can vary from one to eighteen!
According to one calculation there are 1875 ṛks and 2639 sāmas in the Sāmaveda texts available now.
Śākhās of Sāmaveda
As in the case of the other three वेदस्, the Sāmaveda also has several शाखास् (branches or recensions). Though some traditional works like the Caraṇa-vyūha (an appendix to the Atharvaveda) mention that there are a thousand शाखास् in the Sāmaveda, only thirteen names have been discovered so far. They are the names of the teachers who were responsible for re-editing the text and starting their own शाखास्.
Nevertheless, only three such शाखास् are extant now. They are: Jaiminīyaśākhā, Kauthumaśākhā and Rāṇāyanīyaśākhā. The last two have many similarities like equal number of mantras. The first one has 182 mantras less than the other two.
Internal Divisions
The Sāmaveda has two sections called Pūrvārcikā and Uttrārcikā. (Arcikā means a group of ṛks.) The Pūrvārcikā has several prapāṭhakas or chapters containing a few daśatis (decads, though sometimes the number of ṛks is either more or less than ten). The daśatis, again, comprise of ṛks.
The Uttarārcikā has nine prapā-ṭhakas. These are divided into khaṇḍas, each of which consists of a large number of ṛks.
In the Pūrvārcikā, the mantras taken from the Ṛgveda have been regrouped according to the devatā or the deity praised. The first prapāṭhaka contains mantras connected with अग्नि and hence called Āgneyakāṇda. Prapāṭhakas 2 to 4 are known as Aindrakāṇḍa since they are devoted to इन्द्र, the king of gods. The fifth prapāṭhaka contains mantras dedicated to the god सोम-Pavamāna and hence called Pavamānaparva. Most of these mantras have been taken from the ninth मण्डल of the Ṛgveda which itself is entirely devoted to that deity.
The ṛks of these five prapāṭhakas are known as veyagāna or grāmagāna (or grāme geya), because they are to be sung in grāmas or villages and towns. The other terms by which they are known are: chandārcikā, प्रकृति, prakṛtisaṁhitā, and ṛk.
These mantras are used more in ब्रह्मयज्ञ (reciting and teaching the वेदस्), उपाकर्म (See UPĀKARMA.) and certain other rituals. Their use in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् is limited.
The sixth prapāṭhaka is called Araṇyakāṇḍa or Āraṇyakaparva. These mantras have to be chanted in an araṇya or forest, since they are conducive to contemplation.
The ten ṛks appearing at the end of this section are known as महानाम्नी. They are like an appendix to the Pūrvār-cikā. Known also as Śakvaryaḥ—their deity is Indra—they are generally used on the 5th day of the sacrifice.
Since these mantras are addressed to इन्द्र as God, the mahān (= supreme or great), they have come to be known as महानाम्नी.
In the Uttarārcikā, there are nine prapāṭhakas. Each prapāṭhaka has several khaṇḍas (like the daśatis of the Pūrvār-cikā) which contain the ṛks.
The chanting or singing of these ṛks is divided into two groups: ūhagāna and ūhyagāna or rahasyagāna. The basic models for these two are, respectively, the grāmagāna and the araṇyagāna.
There is a repetition of 267 mantras of the Pūrvārcikā in this. The mantras of this section are used in स्तोम (a kind of repetitive prayer) in yajñas or sacrifices. (See also STOMA.)

Methods of Sāmagāna
As already stated, there are four groups of sāmas: grāmageya, āraṇyaka, ūha and ūhya.
The first two are the prakṛtis (basics) and the last two, the vikṛtis (derivatives).
Any मन्त्र taken from the Ṛgveda (a ṛk), when set to मुसिच् as per the system of svaras or notes of the सामवेद, becomes a sāma. This system has been explained in the famous work Nāradīyaśikṣā. According to this work there are 7 svaras (musical notes), 3 grāmas (scales of music—lower range, middle range and top range, respectively called mandrasthāyī, madhyamasthāyī and tārasthāyī), 21 mūrchanas (variation of the notes in an orderly manner) and 49 tānas (protracted notes).
The seven notes of sāmagāna are the equivalents of the seven notes of Indian मुसिच् as shown in the following table:
Sāmasvara Saṅgīta-svara
1. prathama madhyama ma
2. dvitīya gāndhāra ga
3. tṛtīya ṛṣabha ri
4. caturtha ṣaḍja sa
5. pañcama or atisvārya niṣāda ni
6. ṣaṣṭha or mandra daivata da
7. saptama or kruṣṭa pañcama pa

While singing the ṛks as sāma (set to मुसिच्), certain changes are effected in the letters of the text to facilitate singing. They are listed as follows:
1. vikāra Changing the letter or the word; for example ‘agne’ becomes ‘ognāyi’.
2. viśleṣaṇa Separating a word; for example ‘vītaye’ is changed as ‘voyi toyā 2 yi’
3. vikarṣaṇa Lengthening and varying a note; for instance, ‘ye’ is sung as ‘yā 23 yi’.
4. abhyāsa Repetition of a word, as in ‘toyāyi’ which is sung twice.
5. virāma stopping near a word for slight rest,, as for example in ‘gṛṇāno havyadātaye’, stopping before ‘ha’.
6. stobha Certain letters used to embellish singing, like au, hovā and hāvu.

The numbers like 2, 23 etc., indicate the mātrās or time-units needed for chanting at that place.
There are five fundamental steps in the singing of every sāma. They are:
1. prastāva This is the beginning of the मन्त्र. The प्रस्तोतृ priest begins with the sound ‘hum’.
2. udgītha The main priest उद्गातृ sings this, beginning it with

Om.
3

. pratihāra Sung by the priest prati-hartṛ, this part generally expresses a sense of dedi-cation to the deity to whom it is addressed.
4. upadrava This is sung by the उद्गातृ priest himself.
5. nidhana Comprising the last part of the mantra—sometimes including the Om also—this is sung by all the three priests mentioned above,, bringing it to a close.

Some more information may now be adduced here about the sāmas for further elucidation.
The mantras of the Purvārcikā are prakṛtis or basic role models. Each of the ṛks generally has only one sāma, though there are exceptions where the number of sāmas can go up to 18. All the sāmas on the ṛks are already fixed by tradition. Some ṛks may not have any sāma at all. Again, the ṛks sung as sāma may be in any of the well-known metres like गायत्री, anuṣṭubh, triṣṭubh, जगती etc.
Sometimes, the same ṛk can be sung as a sāma in all the four groups beginning with veyagāna.
Some ṛks like punānaḥ सोम dhārayā (Sāmaveda 511) have as many as 61 sāmagānas!
The sāmas (mantras of the Sāmaveda) have been grouped in different ways and have been given different nomenclatures.
The प्रकृति (the first two sections of the pūrvārcikā) has seven types of gānas.
They are: Gāyatragāna (based on the famous gāyatrīmantra); Āgneyagāna (containing ṛks pertaining to अग्नि); Aindra-gāna (with ṛks on इन्द्र in several metres); Pavamānagāna (with ṛks on सोम-Pavamāna); Parvatrayagāna (containing ṛks on Arka [here, अग्नि], couplets called dvandva and vratas); Śukriyagāna (with ṛks on शुक्र or sun)’ and, महानाम्नी (explained already).
The names of some of the other sāmas are: Amṛtasaṁhitā, Ariṣṭavarga, पवित्र-varga, Pitṛsaṁhitā, Skandasaṁhitā, Vaināyakasaṁhitā and so on.
Bṛhatsāma, रथन्तरसाम, Vairāja-sāma, Vāmadevyasāma—these are a few of the other sāmas mentioned in works like the उपनिषद्स्.
Ṛṣis, छन्दस् and Devatās
Anyone wishing to study the Vedic mantras, or even recite them, must know three things about them. They are: ṛṣi (the sage to whom it was revealed), छन्दस् (the metre in which it is composed) and devatā (the deity to whom it is addressed.)
Since the mantras of the Sāmaveda have been taken mostly from the Ṛgveda it can be presumed that the ṛṣi is the first sage to whom the sāma-pattern was originally revealed.
The following are some of the ṛṣis and the number of sāma-mantras revealed to them given in terms of daśatis: Bhāra-dvāja (29); गोतम (20); जमदग्नि (13); कण्व (29); मेधातिथि (29); Praskaṇva (13); Saubhari (18); शुनश्शेफ (17); वामदेव (36); वसिष्ठ (43); विश्वामित्र (29).
Though छन्दस् means the metre, etymologically speaking, it is interpreted as something that covers and hence protects, as also gives joy. A knowledge of the छन्दस् is necessary for the knowledge of the पदपाठ (breaking the words of the sentences and the compound words) which is very important in this Veda.
The following are the Vedic metres used here: anuṣṭubh; बृहती; जगती; paṅkti; triṣṭubh; uṣṇik.
The देवतास् or the presiding deities of the various Sāmavedic mantras are: अग्नि, इन्द्र, प्रजापति, सोम, वरुण, त्वष्टा, Aṅgirasa, Pūṣā, सरस्वती and Indrāgnī.
Subsidiaries of the Sāmaveda
Apart from the Saṁhita, every Veda has three more parts: ब्राह्मण, Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad.
To facilitate its study, the help of the वेदाङ्गस् is also necessary.
A list of these, belonging to the Sāmaveda may now be given:
Brāhmaṇas
Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa;
Devatādhyāya Brāhmaṇa;
Prauḍha Brāhmaṇa,, also known as Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa and Pañcaviṁśa Brāhmaṇa;
Ṣaḍviṁśa Brāhmaṇa;
Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa;
Saṁhitopaniṣad Brāhmaṇa;
Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa;
Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa;
Vaṁśa Brāhmaṇa.
The Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa is the most important of these.
A Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa is also available but only in parts. However it also is considered important.
Āraṇyakas
There is only one Āraṇyaka available called Talavakāra Āraṇyaka. It is a part of the Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa.
Upaniṣads
The Chāndogya and the Kena or Talavakāra Upaniṣads are the major उपनिषद्स् of the Sāmaveda.
Other Upaniṣads—considered as minor ones—are: Aruṇopaniṣad; Jābāladarśa-nopaniṣad; Jābālyupaniṣad; Mahopaniṣad; Vāsudevopaniṣad.
Vedāṅgas
The वेदाङ्गस् dealing exclusively with the Sāmaveda can be listed as follows:
Pāṇinīya Śikśā; Nāradīya Śikśā; Gautama Śikśā; Lomaśa Śikśā; Puṣpa-sūtras; Ṛktantra.
Nidānasūtra of पतञ्जलि and Anupadasūtra of गार्ग्य deal with the छन्दस् or metres of the Sāmavedic mantras.
The श्रौतसूत्रस् of Sāmaveda are: Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtras; Jaiminīya Śrautasūtras; Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtras.
Gobhila Gṛhyasūtras and Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtras belong to the gṛhyasūtra group of the Sāmaveda.
As regards the धर्मसूत्रस् of the Sāmaveda, the Gautama Dharmasūtras is the only ancient work that is extant now.
Quite a few other ancient and medieval works dealing with the subjects of the Sāmaveda are also available.
THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE SĀMAVEDA
Since the Sāmaveda contains only the mantras of the Ṛgveda set to मुसिच्, it has no philosophy of its own, but that of the Ṛgveda itself. However, quite a few of the sāmas bespeak a high kind of भक्ति or devotion. Some of these sentiments may be summarised as follows:
God is brilliant light. May he light up our hearts! (Sāmaveda, Āgneyakāṇḍa 1.1)
O God! Please accept the offerings of our good deeds. (ibid 1.2)
You are our dear friend, respected guest. You take us in the path of bliss and auspiciousness. I pray to you. (ibid 1.5)
O Lord! All speech, hymns of praise, hymns describing your greatness will ultimately merge in your holy feet. (ibid

)
May the spiritual aspirant think of the Supreme Lord, the Being of Light, in his own heart, thereby gaining in faith and the strength to do good deeds! (ibid

)
God as अग्नि destroys our sins and इग्नोरन्चे and enlightens us. (ibid 1.4)
O God as अग्नि! The योगि realises your greatness through divine wisdom.
O singers of the sāmas! Praise the all-powerful God, the destroyer of all sins! We too will eulogise him, the omniscient Lord, the dear friend of all!
O Effulgent God! The ever youthful, the brilliant, the compassionate one! Please shine in our hearts!
O Supreme Lord! You have two forms, one of brilliant splendour and the other of great peace, fit for contemplation. You are the gracious protector of the universe.
We have infinite faith in that creator of the world, who is the dispeller of all sorrow, the best of leaders, the eternal, the all-pervading, the giver of light and the great protector as also the omniscient.
None can vanquish that devotee of God who has surrendered himself to him.
O God! Give us all that we need for our welfare here and destroy all fear brought out by our wrong decisions.
May the all-knowing God, the destroyer of all our troubles, the indweller in the hearts of all, the all-merciful one, lead us in the straight path!
Epilogue
Though the Sāmaveda is, comparatively speaking, a smaller work than the other वेदस्, it has endeared itself to all by its sweet मुसिच्, high literary value (as excellent poetry) and noble sentiments of devotion.
It is, undoubtedly, the origin of Indian classical मुसिच्, though very difficult to master.
It definitely needs more effective propagation and the sāmagas—singers of the sāmas—greater encouragement.

śamī
(‘that which brings peace’)
------------------------------------------
The शमी (Acacia suma) has been considered a holy tree since ages. The Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (6.9.2) contains a prayer addressed to the शमी tree for the removal of sins and enmities. The plant or even a branch is supposed to have the power to appease the terrible and angry aspects of the deities (Vide Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa

.11) like अग्नि.
When a क्षत्त्रिय king intends to go on a victory expedition to subdue or destroy sinners and evil persons, he is expected to worship the शमी tree before starting.
This is performed as a ritual also on the विजयदशमी day (Āśvayuja-śukla-daśamī, generally during October) by क्षत्त्रिय kings even today.
Its leaves are sent to friends and relatives as a sign of goodwill on the विजयदशमी day.
The upper अरणि (See ARAṆI.) is usually prepared out of शमी wood.

samanu
(‘with मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
‘Manu’ means a मन्त्र (holy syllable). Works on हठयोग describe various processes of प्राणायाम for नाडीशुद्धि (purification of the tubular structures through which prāṇic energy flows). Very often, certain bījamantras (seed-letters) like yaṁ, raṁ and ṭhaṁ, are associated with the different stages of these prāṇāyāmas. Hence they are called ‘samanu’ (prāṇāyāmas with bījamantras) (vide Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā 5.36-45).
The actual processes have to be learnt personally from expert teachers.

Sambandhavārttika
(‘brief commentary on the relation’)
------------------------------------------
Sureśvara (A.
) was one of the four chief disciples of शङ्कर (A.

-820). He has written two vārttikas or sub-commentaries on the bhāṣyas of शङ्कर on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
The first one is one of the longest works (spread over 11,151 verses) in इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. The introductory part of it consisting of 1135 verses is known as Sambandhavārttika. It tries to establish the sambandha or relation between the कर्मकाण्ड portion and the ज्ञानकाण्ड portion of the Veda (which deal with rituals and knowledge respectively).
The work is highly polemical.

samiti
(‘assembly’)
------------------------------------------
This is an ancient word used even in the Ṛgveda (10.191.3) and seems to mean a meeting or a meeting place.
It might have been an ad hoc assembly of people attended by learned men and others including the king.
Whether it was a regular national assembly of a whole people, as suggested by some scholars, is a moot point.
The word सभा also might have meant the same.
See SABHĀ.

sāmānya
(‘that which is the same,’ ‘generality’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the seven padārthas or categories recognised by the Vaiśeṣika-दर्शन. See VAIŚEṢIKA-DARŚANA for details.
In the Alaṅkāraśāstra (the science of figure of speech), सामान्य refers to such an element which exists both in the basic object and the object with which it is compared, without any distinction.

Śambarāsura
------------------------------------------
He was one of the four sons of दक्ष from his wife Danu (and hence a dānava or demon by nature) and lived in पाताल (nether world).
See PRADYUMNA for more details.

samārohaṇa
(‘making [the fire] ascend’)
------------------------------------------
If an āhitāgni—one who had ceremonially established a Vedic fire—wanted to go on a पिल्ग्रिमगे, he could put out the fire by the site of समारोहण and re-establish it after returning.
In समारोहण, the आहिताग्नि had to warm his hands on the गार्हपत्य fire (with appropriate mantras) causing अग्नि to enter into his body. Alternatively, it could be done by warming the araṇis and another piece of wood which will be the subtle dwelling place for it till he returns.
When the same process is carried out to establish the fire (once established) elsewhere, it is called समारोपण.

samudramathana
(‘churning of the ocean [of milk]’)
------------------------------------------
Indra, the king of gods, lost his all to the demons, due to the disrespect shown out of pride, to a great sage दुर्वासस्. Lord विष्णु advised him to make up with his enemies (the demons) and with their help, to churn the ocean of milk, out of which अमृत (ambrosia) could be got. By drinking it, the gods could become immortal and regain their lost sovereignty. Accordingly, the gods and the demons started churning the ocean, making the मन्दर mountain as the churning rod and वासुकि, the great serpent as the rope. विष्णु took the form of a gigantic tortoise (Kūrma) to support the mount मन्दर from sinking. The first product of this joint venture and adventure was हालाहल, the most deadly poison! शिव the auspicious one, swallowed this, thus saving the worlds from sure destruction. Then were produced कामधेनु (the wish-yielding cow), उच्चैश्रवस् (the white horse), ऐरावत (the elephant), Kaustubhamaṇi (the matchless jewel), Kalpavṛkṣa (the wish fulfilling tree), लक्ष्मी (the goddess of fortune), Surā or वारुणी (the goddess of wine) and धन्वन्तरि (the physician of the gods) bearing the vessel of अमृत (the ambrosia) in his hands. The Ṛṣis took away the cow कामधेनु, बलि (the king of demons) cast his eye on the horse उच्चैश्रवस्, इन्द्र (the king of gods) accepted the elephant ऐरावत and got the tree Kalpavṛkṣa planted in his garden in हेअवेन्. विष्णु chose to wear the jewel कौस्तुभ on his chest whereas लक्ष्मी chose विष्णु’s chest as her dwelling. The gods chose Surā who had been strangely enough, rejected by the demons. Contravening the original agreement that the अमृत should be shared by both the groups equally, the demons forcibly snatched away the pot from धन्वन्तरि’s hands to appropriate the entire quantity for themselves. Selfishness and greed, however, led to disagreement, discontent and conflict. Taking this opportunity विष्णु took the form of मोहिनी, the enchantress, lured the vessel of ambrosia into his hands and cleverly managed to distribute its contents among the gods only. Then the inevitable happened. Being intoxicated by the new strength gained thus, the gods fell upon the demons, vanquished them and regained their lost sovereignty.
This myth has great lessons for us. In order to get the greatest good of the greatest number, the saner elements of the society should influence the masses to bury their hatchet, sink all their petty differences and make a coordinated and co-operative effort to achieve it. Since the task is stupendous, the effort will have to be equally stupendous. The early results of all such joint ventures need not always be good or pleasant. Due to conflict of personalities and clash of interests which naturally arise in the field of joint ventures, it is हालाहल that appears first and not अमृत! This deadly poison starts destroying all the parties involved in the conflicts irrespective of who is right or who is wrong! Hence out of sheer necessity, the entire society should unite and appeal to the leaders to save it. Any true leader of the society, worth the name, will, like शिव the auspicious one, voluntarily and willingly come forward risking his life, to assimilate this poison and save the society from sure destruction. Once these conflicts are resolved and the efforts are redoubled, लक्ष्मी signifying अभ्युदय (well-being, fortune) and अमृत signifying niśsreyasa (moral and spiritual elevation ultimately leading to beatitude) are bound to arise from the firmament of their joint adventure. But, again, contrary to the covenant, if the selfish and belligerent groups of the society try to appropriate to themselves all the fruits of the common labours, God, the law-giver and justice personified, will thwart their efforts. The good shall and will vanquish the evil.
This story can be interpreted at the subjective level also. Anyone who is tired of the vicissitudes of life and is hankering for peace and bliss should seek it only in the highest spiritual enlightenment. अमृत signifies just this enlightenment. To get this, an all-out effort will have to be made. The sense-organs which usually pull the मिन्द् down and create confusion, conflicts and heart-burns, should be tactfully mobilised in this effort even as the demons were used by the gods. Spiritual life is a long struggle. meditation is actually मिन्द्-churning. Hence, this process will inevitably throw up the deadly poison hidden in the recesses of the मिन्द् as passions and prejudices, which try to destroy every process of sādhana (spiritual efforts). An intense and earnest prayer to God, शिव, will save the situation by getting it sublimated. The conquest of Māra by the बुद्ध or Satan by Christ, can be understood in this light. Once the worst is over, the spiritual aspirant will gradually start reaping the benefits of his efforts in the form of सिद्धिस् (powers), psychic or other-wise. Kāmadhenus and Kalpavṛkṣas can mean such powers. This will be crowned with success when he gets a vision of the all-pervading cosmic energy (Lakṣmī) resulting in immortal bliss (amṛta).

samavāya
(‘inherence’)
------------------------------------------
It is one of the saptapadārthas or seven categories put forward by the Vaiśeṣika system.
See VAIŚEṢIKA-DARŚANA.

sāmānyatodṛṣṭa
(‘seen in a general way’)
------------------------------------------
Anumāna or inference is an important pramāṇa or means of knowledge recognised by almost all systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्. The Nyāyadarśana of गौतम (550 B. C.) has further categorised अनुमान into three varieties: पूर्ववत्; शेषवत् and सामान्यतोदृष्ट.
The पूर्ववत् (‘as seen earlier’) inference is that in which we infer an unperceived effect from a perceived cause, as in the case of inferring future rain from the appearance of dark heavy clouds in the sky.
In शेषवत् (‘from the seen [effect] to the unseen [cause]’), the unperceived cause is inferred from a perceived effect, as in the case of inferring of past rain by seeing the swift muddy currents in the river now.
In the सामान्यतोदृष्ट inference, there is no direct cause and effect relationship (as between fire and smoke). The inference is drawn from the universal experience regarding such an incident. For instance, if there is a change of place, there must have been a movement as known from our common experience. Similarly when we see the मोओन् in different positions at long intervals, we infer that it moves, though the actual movement itself is not easily or clearly perceivable (vide Nyāyasūtras

śāmbhavīmudrā
(‘mudrā related to Śambhu [Śiva]’)
------------------------------------------
It is fixing the gaze on the light of the आत्मन्, in the space between the eyebrows (vide Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā 3.64-67), ultimately resulting in आत्मज्ञान. Such a योगि becomes like आदिनाथ (Primeval Lord) or नारायण.
According to another definition it is aiming at ब्रह्मन् inwardly though the gaze of the eyes is fixed outside, but seeing nothing. This technique learnt from a गुरु, through his grace, will lead to the realisation of the Śambhutattva or शिव (Haṭhayogapradīpikā 4.34-37).
The correct methods have to be learnt from a competent गुरु.

samāvartana
(‘return’)
------------------------------------------
Samāvartana means returning from the होउसे of the teacher to one’s own होउसे after duly completing Vedic studies. Since a ceremonial bath was a necessary part of it, it was also known as स्नान and āplavana (both of which mean bathing).
After this rite, the brahmacāri came to be known as a स्नातक (one who has undergone the ceremonial bathing). He was now free to marry a suitable girl and settle down as a गृहस्थ or householder.
For the समावर्तन rite, an auspicious day had to be fixed. Permission of the गुरु (preceptor) had to be sought after offering him suitable दक्षिणा (gifts).
He should then take the ceremonial bath by taking water from eight vessels (full of water) kept in the eight directions, chanting the prescribed mantras. After this bath, he has to cast off his old outfit completely and put on new clothes more comfortable and suitable for a householder’s life. He could also accept ornaments, turban, umbrella, shoes, flower-garlands and so on, all of which had been forbidden till now!
Dressed in his new attire, the स्नातक was expected to go to an assembly of the learned and prove his competence as a scholar.
A स्नातक commanded great respect and there was a strict code of conduct prescribed for him.
In the modern days, the rite of समावर्तन is observed just before मर्रिअगे, as a formal ritual shorn of its meaning and seriousness as Kāśīyātrā.
See also SNĀTAKA.
